newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican general arrested in new drug scandal.
newsitem.headline: Mexican general arrested in new drug scandal.

text.p: Mexican authorities on Monday jailed an army general on charges he sought to pay $1 million a month in bribes on behalf of a major drug cartel, dealing a fresh blow to Mexico's drugs trade.
It was the second arrest of a Mexican army general in just over a month, and occurred amid a blitz of bad publicity in the United States for Mexico's anti-drugs efforts.

Brigadier General Alfredo Navarro Lara sought to bribe a colleague in the northwestern state of Baja California to turn a blind eye to drug shipments, and threatened to kill him and his family if he refused, the attorney general's office said in a statement.

Navarro Lara, it said, acted as an envoy of the Arellano Felix brothers, heads of the so-called Tijuana Cartel in Baja California, one of the country's most powerful cocaine-smuggling operations across the U.S. border.
It gave no details of the one-star general's background.

According to the statement, in early March Navarro Lara met in a plush hotel in the northern city of Tijauna with Jose Luis Chavez Garcia, a fellow general and the attorney general's representative in the state, and sought to tempt him with the offer.
"In the message, Navarro Lara indicated (to Chavez Garcia) that if he did not accept, he and his family would be executed," it said.
"He also mentioned that the Arellano Felix are perfectly structured and organised and they cannot be arrested because they are supported both in the United States and Mexico."

Navarro Lara warned Chavez Garcia that the last official who turned down such a bribe, Baja California anti-drugs police chief Ernesto Ibarra Santes, was gunned down with three colleagues in Mexico City in September, the statement said. That crime had to date been unsolved.

Chavez Garcia turned a deaf ear to the threat and turned Navarro Lara in -- "an honest and courageous act by another member of the Mexican army," the statement said. Navarro Lara was taken to Mexico's top security prison of Almoloya de Juarez outside Mexico City.

The general's arrest was a second major setback for the military, which has recently taken a higher-profile role in fighting drugs because the country's police forces are widely considered too corrupt.

The scandal also offered fresh ammunition to critics of Mexico in the U.S. Congress, who have launched a campaign to blacklist the country's anti-drugs efforts despite the official blessing of U.S. President Bill Clinton.

In February Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, head of Mexico's National Institute for Combatting Drugs, was arrested on drug corruption charges, the highest-ranking Mexican official ever to be held for such a crime.
Rebollo's arrest stunned Washington and caused critics of Mexico to suggest drug corruption had tainted top levels of its government.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo meanwhile argued the arrest showed he was serious about rooting out the drugs menace, however high up it extended.

Last week, the House of Representatives voted to give Mexico 90 days to improve its drugs performance, threatening if it did not to overturn the White House's "certification" of Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs.
The Senate was expected to act on the issue this week. The Clinton administration on Monday presented a proposal to key senators seeking to head off any dissatisfaction with Mexico.
The Mexican government says decertification, if it were backed up by legal action, would be a violation of the country's sovereignty.
